name: STM32G474RET6
title: STM32G474xB/xC/xE Arm Cortex-M4 microcontrollers with FPU, 170 MHz, 128 to 512 Kbytes Flash, 128 Kbytes SRAM, HRTIM 184 ps, five 12-bit ADCs, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: A Cortex-M4 microcontroller with a single-precision FPU, DSP instructions and an MPU, clocked at up to 170 MHz (213 DMIPS) and running from 1.71 V to 3.6 V. It has 128, 256 or 512 Kbytes of dual-bank ECC Flash, 128 Kbytes of SRAM split 80 + 16 + 32 (the 32 Kbyte block is CCM SRAM on the instruction and data buses), CORDIC and FMAC maths accelerators, a high-resolution timer with 184 ps steps on 12 outputs, and a dense analog set: five 12-bit ADCs, seven DAC channels, seven comparators, six op-amps and a reference buffer. Interfaces include three FDCANs, a full-speed USB device, a Type-C/PD controller, four I2Cs, four SPIs, five U(S)ARTs, an LPUART, a SAI, Quad-SPI and, on 100 pins and up, an FSMC. STM32G474RET6 is the 512 Kbyte LQFP64 part for -40 to 85 °C ambient, with 52 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU, MPU and DSP instructions, up to 170 MHz, 213 DMIPS
128, 256 or 512 Kbytes Flash with ECC, two banks read-while-write; 128 Kbytes SRAM (80 + 16 + 32 CCM)
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; VDDA 1.62 V to 3.6 V; VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V
five 12-bit SAR, 4 Msps at full resolution, up to 42 channels, 16-bit by oversampling
7 channels: 3 buffered external at 1 Msps, 4 unbuffered internal at 15 Msps
7 rail-to-rail comparators, 6 op-amps with PGA, VREFBUF 2.048 / 2.5 / 2.95 V
4 to 48 MHz crystal, 32 kHz crystal, HSI16 ±1%, LSI 32 kHz ±5%, HSI48 with clock recovery
up to 107 fast I/Os; 52 on LQFP64; some 5 V tolerant

pins.name: VBAT
pins.function: Backup supply, 1.55 V to 3.6 V, for the RTC, LSE oscillator and backup registers while VDD is absent.

pins.name: PC13
pins.function: FT I/O. Alternate functions: EVENTOUT, TIM1_BKIN, TIM1_CH1N, TIM8_CH4N. Additional: WKUP2, RTC_TAMP1, RTC_TS, RTC_OUT1. PC13, PC14 and PC15 take their supply through the backup power switch, which sinks only 3 mA: as outputs they run at 2 MHz at most into 30 pF at most, and never source current (no LED drive). After a backup-domain power-up PC13, PC14 and PC15 start as GPIOs; afterwards their role follows the RTC registers, which a system reset leaves untouched.

operation.text: Cortex-M4 at up to 170 MHz with 512 Kbytes of Flash and 128 Kbytes of SRAM in the xE parts, on two AHB and two APB buses joined by a 32-bit multi-AHB matrix. Temperature ranges: -40 to +85 °C ambient (+105 °C junction) or -40 to +125 °C ambient (+130 °C junction), from 1.71 V to 3.6 V. Nine packages from 48 to 128 pins. The FSMC exists only on packages of 100 pins and more.

Arm Cortex-M4 with a single-precision FPU covering all Arm single-precision data-processing instructions and data types, a full DSP instruction set and an MPU. Compatible with the standard Arm toolchain.
A memory accelerator in front of the Flash that hides its wait states from the Cortex-M4, giving zero-wait-state execution at up to 170 MHz.

Up to 8 protected regions, each split into up to 8 subregions, sized from 32 bytes to the full 4 Gbyte space. An access the MPU forbids can be caught by an RTOS, whose kernel may reprogram the regions per task. The MPU can be left unused.

512 Kbytes for code and data, single- or dual-bank; in dual-bank mode one bank can be read while the other is erased or programmed, and boot from either bank is possible. ECC corrects single errors, detects double errors and records the failing address in a register. 1 Kbyte (128 double words) of OTP lives in bank 1 only: written once, never erased.

Readout protection has three levels: 0 none; 1 blocks Flash read and write while debug is attached or when booting from RAM or the bootloader; 2 disables debug (JTAG and SWD), RAM boot and bootloader selection permanently. Write protection blocks erase and program of an area. PCROP makes an area execute-only for the CPU, refusing DMA, debug and data access; option bit PCROP_RDP selects whether that area is erased when RDP drops from level 1 to 0. A securable area, set by option bytes, behaves as normal Flash until secured; afterwards any access to it returns an error until the next reset, so code and keys in it run once at boot.

128 Kbytes in three blocks: SRAM1, 80 Kbytes at 0x2000 0000, with parity on its first 32 Kbytes, reached on the system bus (or I-Code/D-Code when booting from it or remapped by SYSCFG_MEMRMP); SRAM2, 16 Kbytes at 0x2001 4000 on the system bus, can be kept through Standby; CCM SRAM, 32 Kbytes at 0x1000 0000 on I-Code/D-Code for the fastest CPU access, also aliased at 0x2001 8000 so every master (CPU, DMA1, DMA2) sees it right after SRAM2, with parity and write protection in 1 Kbyte steps. All of it runs at full CPU clock with no wait states.

A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix links the masters (CPU I-bus, D-bus and S-bus, DMA1, DMA2) to the slaves (Flash through the accelerator, SRAM1, CCM SRAM, SRAM2, AHB1 and AHB2 peripherals, FSMC and QUADSPI) so several fast transfers can run at once.

The BOOT0 pin, or the nBOOT0 option bit when option bit nBOOT_SEL frees the PB8-BOOT0 pad, together with option bit nBOOT1 selects boot from user Flash, system memory or embedded SRAM. The system-memory bootloader reprograms Flash over USART, I2C, SPI or USB DFU.

Hardware for trigonometric and related functions: 24-bit engine in circular and hyperbolic, rotation and vectoring modes; functions sin, cos, atan, atan2, modulus and sqrt, hyperbolic sinh, cosh and atanh, and ln; precision up to 20 bits at 4 bits per clock; 16-bit or 32-bit fixed-point in and out; results readable as soon as ready without polling; DMA read and write channels.

A filter accelerator with a 16 x 16-bit multiplier and 24+2-bit accumulator (add and subtract), 16-bit data, and 256 x 16-bit local memory holding up to three buffers (two in, one out) set by base pointers and sizes. Buffers may be circular, with a watermark to cut interrupt load. Runs FIR and IIR (direct form 1) filters; AHB slave with DMA read and write channels.

Computes a CRC with programmable polynomial value and size, for checking stored or transmitted data, including a Flash signature at run time compared against one made at link time (as EN/IEC 60335-1 allows).

VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V feeds the I/Os, the regulator and the system analog (reset, power management, internal clocks). VDDA 1.62 V to 3.6 V feeds the ADCs, DACs, VREFBUF, op-amps and comparators; it is independent of VDD and best tied to VDD when those blocks are unused (the minimum VDDA each block needs is in the electrical characteristics). VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V feeds the RTC, the 32 kHz oscillator and the backup registers through a power switch when VDD is absent.

VREF+ is the ADC and DAC reference input, and the VREFBUF output when the buffer is on. With VDDA below 2 V, VREF+ must equal VDDA; at 2 V and above, it must lie between 2 V and VDDA. VREFBUF offers 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.95 V, chosen by the VRS bits of VREFBUF_CSR. VREF- is bonded to VSSA.

An ultra-low-power BOR runs in every mode but Shutdown and holds the part in reset while VDD is below threshold, so no external reset circuit is needed; its lowest level is 1.71 V at power-on and higher levels are set in option bytes. The PVD, enabled in software, compares VDD with VPVD and can interrupt when VDD falls below or rises above it. A peripheral voltage monitor checks VDDA against a fixed threshold.

Two linear regulators feed the core logic: the main regulator (MR) in Run and Sleep, the low-power regulator (LPR) in Stop and in both low-power run and sleep modes; both are off with high-impedance outputs in Standby and Shutdown. VCORE scales with the maximum frequency: Range 1 boost up to 170 MHz, Range 1 normal up to 150 MHz, Range 2 up to 26 MHz.

Run after any reset. Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals keep running and wake it by interrupt or event. Low-power run puts VCORE on the LPR with the CPU at 2 MHz at most, code from SRAM or Flash, and independent-clock peripherals on HSI16. Low-power sleep is entered from Low-power run, stops the CPU clock and returns to Low-power run on wakeup. Stop keeps SRAM and registers, stops all VCORE clocks and turns off the PLL, HSI16 and HSE; LSE or LSI keeps running and the RTC may stay on; some wakeup-capable peripherals can turn HSI16 on during Stop to handle the event.

Standby turns the regulator off, powers down the PLL, HSI16 and HSE, keeps BOR active, and loses SRAM and registers except the RTC domain and standby logic (SRAM2 can be kept); each I/O can hold a pull-up, pull-down or nothing. Exit by NRST, IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge (rising or falling, selectable), an RTC alarm, wakeup-timer, timestamp or tamper event, or LSE failure (CSS on LSE). Shutdown is lower still: LSI is off too, BOR and all supply monitoring are gone, so switching to the RTC domain is not supported; SRAM and registers are lost except the RTC domain; exit by NRST, IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge or any RTC event. The RTC can stay on in both.
During and after reset the I/Os are in analog state with Schmitt triggers off, to save current, and the internal reset pull-up is turned off when the reset source is internal.

VBAT can come from a battery, a supercapacitor, or VDD when neither battery is fitted and a supercapacitor is present. It keeps the RTC (on LSE) and the backup registers alive, and three tamper pins stay usable. The switch to VBAT happens automatically when VDD goes away, and an internal charger for the VBAT source can be turned on while VDD is present. On VBAT alone, neither external interrupts nor RTC alarms or events bring the device out of VBAT operation.
Peripherals signal each other directly in hardware, without the CPU, with fixed short latency; depending on the link this works in Run, Sleep and Stop.

SYSCLK comes from HSE (4 to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, or an external clock in bypass), HSI16 (16 MHz RC, software-trimmed) or the PLL (fed by HSE or HSI16, 170 MHz maximum). HSI48 (48 MHz RC with clock recovery) can clock USB or the RNG. The RTC runs from LSE (32.768 kHz crystal with four drive levels, or bypass) or LSI (32 kHz, ±5%, also clocking the IWDG). I2S, USART, I2C, LPTIM, ADC, SAI and RNG can run on clocks independent of SYSCLK. AHB, APB1 and APB2 each have a prescaler and run at up to 170 MHz. Clock sources can be switched on the fly.

If HSE fails, the CSS moves SYSCLK to HSI16 and can raise an interrupt; an LSE failure can also be detected with an interrupt. MCO puts one internal clock out on a pin; LSCO puts out LSI or LSE in every low-power mode.

Each pin is an output (push-pull or open-drain), an input (floating, pulled up or pulled down) or an alternate function; most share digital or analog functions. The GPIOs sit on AHB2 for fast toggling. The alternate-function setup can be locked by a set write sequence against stray writes.

Two controllers, DMA1 and DMA2, with 8 channels each (16 in all), each channel tied to a hardware request with software trigger also possible. Four software priority levels per controller, ties settled by channel number. Byte, half-word or word transfers with independent source and destination sizes (packing and unpacking; addresses aligned to size), circular buffers, any direction between memory and peripherals (including memory to memory and peripheral to peripheral), with Flash, SRAM and AHB or APB peripherals as source or destination. Half-transfer, transfer-complete and error flags share one interrupt per channel. Up to 65536 data per transfer.

A request router connects peripheral DMA request lines to the DMA channels, each channel picking one request either freely or in step with synchronisation inputs; a built-in request generator makes DMA requests from trigger events.

16 priority levels and up to 102 maskable interrupt channels beside the 16 Cortex-M4 lines, with low-latency entry, the vector address handed straight to the core, late-arrival handling, tail chaining and automatic state saving.

44 edge-detector lines raise interrupts or events and wake the device from Stop. Each line has its own trigger choice (rising, falling or both) and mask, and a pending register; pulses shorter than an internal clock period are caught. Internal lines come from peripherals that can wake from Stop. Up to 107 GPIOs map onto the 16 external lines.

Five SAR ADCs, 12-bit native with built-in calibration; 4 Msps at full resolution with sampling down to 25 ns, faster at lower resolution (up to 6.66 Msps at 6 bits). One external reference pin on every package. Single-ended or differential inputs. Current falls linearly with conversion rate, and a dual clock domain decouples ADC speed from CPU speed. Sequencer with regular and injected groups, single, continuous or discontinuous scans, multiple timer and external triggers, results to a register or by DMA to RAM, alignment and per-channel offset, hardware oversampling for SNR, per-channel sampling time, analog watchdogs that interrupt or trigger timers, injected-context queue, and hardware gain and offset compensation.

The sensor gives a voltage VTS linear with temperature, read through an internal ADC channel. Its offset differs from chip to chip, so uncalibrated it suits relative measurement only; each part carries two factory readings (TS_CAL1 at 30 °C, TS_CAL2 at 110 °C) in read-only system memory.
A bandgap reference for the ADC and comparators, on internal channel ADCx_IN18 for x = 1, 3, 4, 5. Its exact value at 30 °C, VDDA = VREF+ = 3.0 V, is measured per part and stored in system memory.
Each op-amp output OPAMPxINT (x = 1 to 6) can be sampled on an internal ADC channel, which frees the I/O its output would otherwise use for GPIO.

Seven 12-bit channels, three buffered to pins and four unbuffered internal, built from resistor strings and an inverting amplifier. 8- or 12-bit modes, left or right alignment in 12-bit, buffer offset calibration (factory and user), synchronised update, noise, triangle and sawtooth generation, dual-channel independent or simultaneous conversion, DMA per channel, external triggers, and a low-power sample-and-hold whose capacitor may be on-chip or external. 1 Msps maximum on a pin output and 15 Msps internally. Timer update outputs trigger conversions.

A buffered reference for the ADCs, DACs and external parts on VREF+, at 2.048 V, 2.5 V or 2.9 V; the third level is also stated as 2.95 V. With the buffer off, an external reference can drive VREF+. On packages that bond VREF+ to VDDA the buffer cannot be used. A 100 nF low-frequency cut-off capacitor sits on VREF+.

Seven rail-to-rail comparators with programmable hysteresis. The reference input is an I/O, a DAC channel, or VREFINT or a fraction of it (1/4, 1/2, 3/4). Every comparator can wake the device from Stop, interrupt, and generate timer breaks.
Six op-amps, rail-to-rail in and out, 15 MHz bandwidth, with external or internal follower routing and a PGA: non-inverting gains 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or inverting gains -1, -3, -7, -15, -31, -63.
A true random number generator built on an analog circuit, delivering 32-bit numbers.

The timer set: HRTIM; TIM1, TIM8 and TIM20 for motor control; TIM2, TIM3, TIM4, TIM5, TIM15, TIM16 and TIM17 for general use (up to seven); TIM6 and TIM7 as basic timers; LPTIM1; the IWDG and WWDG watchdogs; and SysTick.

One master and six slave timers giving 12 high-resolution outputs that pair up for dead time. A 170 MHz digital core feeds closed-loop delay lines that hold 184 ps resolution across voltage, temperature and process, on all 12 outputs, in variable-duty, variable-frequency and constant-on-time modes. Six fault inputs and ten external-event inputs (current limit, zero voltage or zero current switching). Blanking and filtering of spurious events, DMA requests, a burst-mode controller, push-pull and resonant modes. Slave timers combine for multi-switch converters or run separate converters: LLC, phase-shifted full bridge, buck, boost in voltage or current mode, lighting; also usable as a general timer or a PWM-based DAC. In debug the counters freeze and outputs go to a safe state.

TIM1, TIM8 and TIM20: four-phase PWM on 8 channels with complementary outputs and programmable dead time. The 4 independent channels do input capture, output compare, edge- or centre-aligned PWM from 0 to 100%, and one-pulse output. In debug the counter can freeze and the PWM outputs turn off, shutting the power switches they drive. They link with the general-purpose timers for synchronisation or chaining.

TIM2 and TIM5: 32-bit up/down counter with 32-bit prescaler. TIM3 and TIM4: 16-bit up/down counter and prescaler. All four have 4 channels for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, their own DMA requests and quadrature-encoder support. TIM15 (2 channels, 1 complementary) and TIM16, TIM17 (1 channel, 1 complementary) have 16-bit up counters and prescalers, with capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse on every channel and their own DMA requests. All link for synchronisation or chaining and freeze in debug.
TIM6 and TIM7 mostly trigger the DAC and also serve as 16-bit time bases.

A 16-bit up counter with 16-bit autoreload and compare, pulse or PWM output, continuous or one-shot, software or hardware trigger, digital glitch filter and encoder mode. Clocked from LSE, LSI, HSI16 or APB, or from an external signal on its input that needs no internal clock (pulse counting). It keeps running in Stop on LSE, LSI or an external clock and can wake the system.

12-bit down counter with 8-bit prescaler on the 32 kHz LSI, independent of the main clock, so it runs in Stop and Standby. Resets the device on a fault or serves as a free-running timeout timer. Hardware or software start by option byte; freezable in debug.
7-bit down counter on the main clock that can run free and resets the device on a fault, with an early-warning interrupt; freezable in debug.
24-bit down counter with autoreload, a maskable interrupt on reaching 0 and a selectable clock, meant for an RTOS tick or general counting.

BCD calendar with subseconds, seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h), weekday, date, month and year, with automatic month-length and leap-year correction. Two alarms. Shift correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses to align with a master clock. A 50 or 60 Hz reference input sharpens the calendar. Digital calibration in 0.95 ppm steps for crystal error. Timestamp on the timestamp pin, a tamper event or the switch to VBAT. 17-bit auto-reload wakeup timer. Powered from VDD or VBAT through a switch. Clocked by LSE (crystal, resonator or oscillator), LSI (32 kHz typ) or HSE/32. On LSE it works in VBAT mode and every low-power mode; on LSI it works in every low-power mode except Shutdown and not in VBAT mode. Alarms, wakeup timer and timestamp can interrupt and wake the device.

32 backup registers of 32 bits, kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT mode, not cleared by system or power reset or by wakeup from Standby or Shutdown, and erased by any tamper detection. Up to three external tamper pins (edge, edge and level, or filtered level detection) and five internal tamper sources. Any tamper can take an RTC timestamp, interrupt and wake the device from every low-power mode.
IRTIM combines TIM17 channel 1 (carrier) with TIM16 channel 1 (envelope) into IR_OUT, on PB9 or PA13; programming the two output-compare channels gives the standard IR modulation schemes.

Four I2Cs to the I2C-bus specification rev. 5: master and slave, multimaster, Standard-mode 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode 400 kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive, 7- and 10-bit addressing with several 7-bit slave addresses, programmable setup and hold, optional clock stretching. SMBus 2.0 (hardware PEC with ACK control, ARP, alert) and PMBus 1.1. Independent clock so bit rate holds when PCLK changes, wakeup from Stop on address match, programmable analog and digital filtering, and a single-byte data buffer served by DMA.

USART1, USART2 and USART3 plus UART4 and UART5: asynchronous, IrDA SIR, multiprocessor, single-wire half duplex and LIN master/slave, with hardware CTS/RTS and RS485 driver enable. The USARTs add ISO 7816 smartcard and SPI-like synchronous modes. Transmit and receive FIFOs of 8, off by default. Each has a clock domain apart from the CPU and can wake the device from Stop on a start bit, any frame, a chosen frame, or certain FIFO status events. All work with DMA.

One low-power UART: asynchronous, half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS, multiprocessor, with 8-deep FIFOs off by default and its own clock domain. It wakes the device from Stop on a start bit, any frame, a chosen frame or certain FIFO events. From the 32.768 kHz LSE alone it reaches 9600 baud, so it can wait for a frame in Stop at very low energy; faster clocks give higher rates. Works with DMA.

Four SPIs, up to 75 Mbit/s as master and 41 Mbit/s as slave, full duplex, half duplex or simplex, frames of 4 to 16 bits, 3-bit prescaler giving 8 master rates, hardware CRC, TI mode and NSS pulse mode. SPI2 and SPI3 double as I2S (four audio standards, master or slave, half duplex) carrying 16-, 24- or 32-bit frames at 16- or 32-bit resolution, sample rates from 8 kHz to 192 kHz from an 8-bit linear prescaler, and as master a 256 x fs clock output for a codec. All SPIs work with DMA.

One serial audio interface with two independent sub-blocks, each transmitter or receiver with an 8-word FIFO, synchronous or asynchronous to each other, master or slave each, with its own clock generator when both are masters. Data of 8, 10, 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits; protocols I2S, TDM, PCM/DSP, AC'97, MSB- or LSB-justified, and SPDIF output; a frame of as many as 16 slots with selectable active slots; configurable frame length, sync level, offset and width, first-bit position, LSB or MSB first, strobing edge; mute; stereo or mono. Overrun, underrun, early and late frame sync (slave) and AC'97 codec-not-ready flags with interrupts; two DMA channels.

Three CAN modules, FDCAN1 to FDCAN3, to ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0, sharing a 3 Kbyte message RAM that holds filters, receive FIFOs and buffers, transmit event FIFOs and transmit buffers.

Full-speed (12 Mbit/s) USB 2.0 device with internal PHY, built-in DP pull-up, Battery Charging 1.2 detection and Link Power Management. Endpoints configured in software, up to 1 Kbyte of packet memory, suspend and resume. Needs an accurate 48 MHz clock: from the PLL with an HSE crystal, or from HSI48 trimmed automatically from USB SOF, which allows crystal-less operation.

One controller to USB Type-C 1.2 and USB Power Delivery 3.0, on dedicated I/Os with Rp (all values) and Rd resistors, dead-battery support, PD message send and receive and fast role swap. The logic handles Type-C level detection with debounce and interrupts, FRS detection, a byte interface for PD payload (DMA capable), PD timing dividers with prescaler, CRC, 4b5b coding, ordered sets with a receive mask, and frequency recovery during the preamble. It keeps detecting PD messages and FRS signalling in Stop.

Trims HSI48 automatically against USB SOF, LSE, an external signal on CRS_SYNC or a software event, holding its accuracy across the operating range; manual trimming can be combined for faster lock at start-up.

Static memory controller (also called FMC) with a NOR/PSRAM controller and a NAND controller: SRAM, NOR and OneNAND Flash, PSRAM in 4 banks, NAND with hardware ECC over up to 8 Kbytes, and FRAM. 8- or 16-bit bus, separate chip select and setup per bank, write FIFO, FMC_CLK up to HCLK/2 for synchronous access. It also drives LCD controllers in Intel 8080 or Motorola 6800 mode.

Interface to single, dual or quad SPI Flash, in indirect, status-polling or memory-mapped mode; dual-flash mode reads two quad memories at once for twice the throughput and capacity. SDR and DDR; programmable opcode and frame format with instruction, address, alternate-byte, dummy and data phases each set for presence, length and 1, 2 or 4 lines. FIFO, 8-, 16- and 32-bit access, DMA in indirect mode, flag masking, timeout, and interrupts on FIFO threshold, timeout, status match, completion and access error.

SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial-wire debug: SWD needs 2 pins (SWDIO shared with JTMS, SWCLK with JTCK), and a sequence on TMS switches between JTAG-DP and SW-DP; unused JTAG pins can be GPIOs. The ETM streams compressed instruction and data trace over a few pins to an external trace port analyser.

PC13, PC14 and PC15 take their supply through the backup power switch, which sinks only 3 mA: as outputs they run at 2 MHz at most into 30 pF at most, and never source current (no LED drive). After a backup-domain power-up PC13, PC14 and PC15 start as GPIOs; afterwards their role follows the RTC registers, which a system reset leaves untouched.
Out of reset these pins carry the JTAG/SW debug functions, with the internal pull-up on PA15, PA13 and PB4 and the internal pull-down on PA14 switched on.
Leaving PB8 unconnected in analog mode costs current; set it to another mode after start-up.
The VSS pads of the UFQFPN48 connect to its exposed pad.

Alternate functions are picked per pin through the GPIOx_AFR registers (AF0 to AF15, port tables); additional functions such as ADC inputs, oscillator pins and wakeup inputs are enabled directly from the peripheral's registers.

Voltages are taken against VSS unless a row says otherwise. Minimum and maximum figures hold over the worst case of ambient temperature, supply and clock and are tested on every part at 25 °C and at the top of the ordered temperature range; figures marked as coming from characterization, design or simulation are not production tested, and a characterized limit is the sample mean plus or minus three standard deviations. A typical figure is at 25 °C with VDD = VDDA = 3 V and is a design guide only, as is every typical curve. A typical ADC accuracy figure is one that 95 % of a sampled lot meets or betters across temperature (mean plus or minus two standard deviations). Pin parameters are measured with 50 pF from the pin to ground, and a pin's input voltage is the voltage from the pin to ground.

Every supply pair (VDD/VSS, VDDA/VSSA and so on) takes ceramic decoupling placed as close to its pins as possible, or on the back of the board under them. The VDD pins take 100 nF each plus one 4.7 µF; VDDA takes 10 nF plus 1 µF; VREF+ takes 100 nF plus 1 µF. VBAT runs from 1.55 V to 3.6 V and feeds the backup domain (LSE, RTC, backup registers) through the internal power switch. The analog blocks (ADCs, DACs, op-amps, comparators, VREFBUF) take their reference from VREF+/VREF-.
Current is measured separately into VBAT (IDD_VBAT), VDD (IDD) and VDDA (IDDA). The IDD_ALL figures of the supply-current tables are the whole chip: the sum of what flows into VDD, VDDA and VBAT.

Going past any figure in the voltage, current or thermal ratings tables can damage the part for good; they are stress limits and the part is not meant to work at them, and long exposure to them can shorten its life. The device's mission profile meets the JEDEC JESD47 qualification standard; longer mission profiles are offered on request.

Supply current depends on supply voltage, ambient temperature, I/O loading, software configuration, clock frequencies, how fast the I/Os switch, where the program runs from and the code itself. For the supply-current tables every I/O is an analog input, every peripheral is off unless named, the Flash runs with the fewest wait states that suit fHCLK (the wait-state table is in reference manual RM0440), fPCLK = fHCLK when peripherals are on, and Range 1 is set to Boost mode for 150 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 170 MHz and to Normal mode for 26 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 150 MHz. Ambient temperature and supply follow the general operating conditions.

I/O current has a static part and a dynamic part. Statically, an input with its pull-up on draws current whenever the pin is held low outside, set by the pull resistor values of the I/O static characteristics table; an output also feeds whatever external pull-down or load hangs on it. An input left at a voltage between the logic levels draws extra current through its Schmitt trigger; configuring such pins as analog avoids it, and ADC, OPAMP and COMP inputs belong in analog mode. A floating input can drift to such a level or toggle from outside noise, so an unused pin is either analog or held at a fixed level by a pull resistor or by making it an output. Dynamically, a switching pin draws current from its I/O supply to run its circuitry and to charge and discharge the load on it; this was measured with the pin a push-pull output toggled by software at a fixed rate.

Each peripheral's figure is the difference in supply current between that peripheral clocked and not clocked, with every I/O in analog mode. It covers only the digital part; the analog part of a peripheral, where it has one, is in that peripheral's own section.
A wakeup time runs from the wakeup event to the first user instruction executed. The figures are taken with the part entering the low-power mode through a WFE instruction.

In bypass mode the HSE or LSE oscillator is off and OSC_IN or OSC32_IN is an ordinary GPIO input; the external clock meets the I/O characteristics, and its high and low times, levels and edges are defined between the 10 % and 90 % points of the waveform, with period THSE or TLSE.

The HSE oscillator runs a 4 MHz to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator. Its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. The resonator and its load capacitors go as near the oscillator pins as possible to limit output distortion and start-up settling time. CL1 and CL2 are high-quality ceramic capacitors for high-frequency use, typically 5 pF to 20 pF, matched to the crystal and normally equal in value. A crystal's rated load capacitance is CL1 and CL2 in series plus the pin and board capacitance, which can be taken as about 10 pF in all. Crystal selection is covered in application note AN2867.

The LSE oscillator runs a 32.768 kHz crystal through a drive-programmable amplifier. Its figures come from design simulation with typical external parts; the crystal and its two load capacitors go as near the OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT pins as possible. No resistor may be fitted between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT: none is needed and adding one is not allowed.
The internal oscillator figures are taken over the general operating conditions; their curves are characterization results and are not tested in production.

Susceptibility is tested on samples during characterization. With a simple program toggling two LEDs, the part is stressed until the LEDs show a fault: electrostatic discharges of both polarities on every pin (IEC 61000-4-2), and bursts of fast transients of both polarities on VDD and VSS through 100 pF (IEC 61000-4-4). A reset brings the part back to normal operation. The levels and classes follow application note AN1709.

EMC is characterized and tuned at component level with a typical board and simple software, and the result in a product depends heavily on its own design and software. Runaway conditions for the software to manage include a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset and corrupted critical data such as control registers. Most of these faults can be reproduced for testing by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s, and ESD can be applied straight to the part within its specified range; software hardening against unrecoverable errors is covered in application note AN1015.
Emission is measured with a simple program toggling two LEDs, on the test board and pin loading set by IEC 61967-2.

ESD: a positive then a negative pulse 1 s apart is applied to each pin combination of each sample; the sample size is 3 parts × (n + 1) supply pins, per the ANSI/JEDEC standard. Latch-up: on three parts, an overvoltage on each supply pin and a current injected into each I/O pin, whether input, output or configurable, per EIA/JESD 78E.

Injecting current into an I/O, from a pin voltage below VSS or above VDD on a 3.3 V-capable pin, is to be avoided in normal use. Robustness against accidental injection is checked on samples during characterization: with a simple program running, current is driven into one floating-input pin at a time while the part is watched for a fault, namely an ADC error above 5 LSB TUE, leakage induced on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA to +0 µA, a reset, or a shift of oscillator frequency. Negative injection induces negative leakage and positive injection positive leakage.

Every I/O meets both CMOS and TTL input levels with no configuration, and beyond the strict figures of either standard. Production-tested limits are VIL max = 0.3 × VDDIO and VIH min = 0.7 × VDDIO; from simulation, VIL max = 0.39 × VDDIO - 0.06 and VIH min = 0.49 × VDDIO + 0.26 for VDDIO above 1.62 V, and VIL max = 0.43 × VDDIO - 0.1 and VIH min = 0.61 × VDDIO + 0.05 for 1.08 V < VDDIO < 1.62 V, against the TTL requirements VIL max = 0.8 V and VIH min = 2 V.

A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA at the standard output levels and up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL and VOH. The number of pins driving current is limited by the absolute maximum ratings: the current all I/Os source from VDD plus the chip's own maximum VDD current stays within ΣIVDD, and the current all I/Os sink into VSS plus the chip's own maximum VSS current stays within ΣIVSS.

Output rise time tr(IO)out runs from 10 % to 90 % of the swing and fall time tf(IO)out from 90 % to 10 %. The maximum frequency is reached when tr + tf ≤ 2/3 T and the duty cycle stays within 45 % to 55 % at the rated load capacitance.

The NRST input is a CMOS stage with a permanent pull-up RPU to VDD, followed by a filter ahead of the internal reset. A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, placed as near the part as possible, guards against parasitic resets. Whatever drives NRST must be able to pull it below the VIL(NRST) maximum, or the reset is missed.

The HRTIM figures hold over the general operating conditions of ambient temperature and supply. Clocked at 170 MHz, the timer steps in 184 ps (typical, -40 to 105 °C); its counters are 16 bits wide; the dead-time generator runs at 0.735 ns to 94.1 ns per step over a range of up to 511 steps (48.09 µs), and the chopper runs at fHRTIM/256 to fHRTIM/16 with a first pulse of 16 to 256 tHRTIM. A fault input reaches the outputs in 9 ns typical from a digital FLT pin and 16 ns from a comparator input, and needs a pulse of at least 7 ns. External events 1 to 5 in low-latency mode reach the outputs in 12 ns (digital) or 19 ns (comparator); events 1 to 10 in synchronous mode take 56 ns or 62 ns with up to one tHRTIM of jitter.
A pulse on an interrupt input is detected by the event controller only if it lasts at least the PLEC minimum.

The ADC figures are preliminary values over the general operating conditions of ambient temperature, fPCLK and VDDA. A calibration after every power-up is advised. Below VDDA = 2.4 V the analog-switch voltage booster on the I/Os is enabled (BOOSTEN = 1 in SYSCFG_CFGR1); from 2.4 V up it is disabled. On some packages VREF+ is tied to VDDA inside. Fast channels are ADCx_IN1 to ADCx_IN5; every other ADC input is a slow channel.

Total unadjusted error ET is the largest gap between the real and the ideal transfer curves. Offset error EO is the gap between the first real code transition and the first ideal one. Gain error EG is how far the last real transition sits from the last ideal one. Differential linearity error ED is the largest departure of a real code step from the ideal 1 LSB. Integral linearity error EL is the largest gap between any real transition and the straight line through the end points. The code axis runs 0 to 4095 against Vin/VREF × 4096.

The source drives an analog input AINx through its own resistance RAIN; the board and pad add Cparasitic to ground, and inside, the pin leakage Ilkg, the sampling switch RADC and the sample-and-hold capacitor CADC lead to the 12-bit converter. Cparasitic is the board capacitance, which depends on soldering and layout, plus the pad capacitance (CIO); a large Cparasitic degrades accuracy, and a lower fADC wins it back. Supply decoupling follows the power supply scheme, with a good-quality ceramic capacitor on VDDA as close to the chip as possible.

Each 12-bit DAC drives DACx_OUT through an output buffer that lowers the output impedance so the pin can drive an external load (RLOAD, CLOAD) directly without an external op-amp. Setting BOFFx in DAC_CR bypasses the buffer.

The timer figures are guaranteed by design. The input and output figures of the timer alternate functions (PWM output, output compare, input capture, external clock) are those of the I/O port characteristics. TIMx stands for TIM1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 15, 16, 17 and 20.

The I2C interfaces meet the timing that revision 03 of the I2C-bus specification sets for Standard-mode (up to 100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (up to 400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (up to 1 Mbit/s). The timing is guaranteed by design when the peripheral is set up as reference manual RM0440 describes and I2CCLK is above the minimum frequency for the mode.

SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS from the pin to VDDIOx is switched off but still there. The 20 mA drive asked for in Fast-mode Plus is only partly met, which caps the bus load Cload in Fm+ through tr(SDA/SCL) = 0.8473 × Rp × Cload and Rp(min) = (VDD - VOL(max)) / IOL(max), Rp being the bus pull-up. Every SDA and SCL I/O has an analog spike filter.

The slave CPHA = 1 and master timing waveforms are referred to 0.3 × VDD and 0.7 × VDD. With CPHA = 0 the slave drives MISO from NSS falling (ta(SO)) and holds each bit th(SO) past the clock edge, with MOSI sampled after tsu(SI) and held th(SI); with CPHA = 1 the same timings refer to the opposite clock edge. In master mode MISO is set up tsu(MI) before and held th(MI) after the sampling edge, and MOSI is valid tv(MO) after the driving edge and held th(MO). The input and output figures of the SPI pins (NSS, SCK, MOSI, MISO) are those of the I/O port characteristics.

fMCK, fCK and DCK reflect the digital peripheral only; the precision of the source clock can shift them slightly. DCK depends mostly on the ODD bit: the digital part alone gives a minimum of I2SDIV/(2 × I2SDIV + ODD) and a maximum of (I2SDIV + ODD)/(2 × I2SDIV + ODD). The sampling frequency Fs and the highest Fs for each mode are in the I2S section of reference manual RM0440. The I/O figures of CK, SD and WS are those of the I/O port characteristics.
The input and output figures of FDCANx_TX and FDCANx_RX are those of the I/O port characteristics.

The USB interface meets USB specification 2.0 in full, and USB-IF has certified it as a full-speed device. USB works down to 2.7 V, but between 2.7 V and 3.0 V its electrical figures are degraded. D+ (USB_DP) and D- (USB_DM) take no series termination resistors, since the on-chip driver already carries the matching impedance.

The FSMC timing tables hold over the general operating conditions of ambient temperature, fHCLK and VDD, with output speed OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD; THCLK is the HCLK period throughout. The asynchronous figures are taken with AddressSetupTime = 0x1, AddressHoldTime = 0x1, DataHoldTime = 0x1, ByteLaneSetup = 0x1, DataSetupTime = 0x1 (0x5 in asynchronous NWAIT mode) and BusTurnAroundDuration = 0x0.

The synchronous figures are taken with burst access on, the CRAM memory type, write burst on, a clock division of 1, and a data latency of 1 for NOR Flash or 0 for PSRAM. For 2.7 V ≤ VDD ≤ 3.6 V with 30 pF on FMC_CLK, FMC_CLK reaches 60 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x1 and 54 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x0; for 1.71 V ≤ VDD ≤ 2.7 V with 20 pF, 60 MHz and 32 MHz.

The NAND figures are taken with COM and ATT SetupTime = 0x01, WaitSetupTime = 0x03, HoldSetupTime = 0x02 and HiZSetupTime = 0x01, Bank = FMC_Bank_NAND, a 16-bit memory data width, ECC on with a 512-byte ECC page, and TCLRSetupTime = TARSetupTime = 0. ALE is on FMC_A17 and CLE on FMC_A16.
UCPD1 follows revision 1.2 of the USB Type-C specification and revision 3.0 of USB Power Delivery.

The STM32G474 comes in nine packages: WLCSP81 (4.02 x 4.27 mm, 0.4 mm ball pitch), UFQFPN48 (7 x 7 mm, 0.5 mm pitch), LQFP48 (7 x 7 mm), LQFP64 (10 x 10 mm), LQFP80 (12 x 12 mm), TFBGA100 (8 x 8 mm, 0.8 mm ball pitch), LQFP100 (14 x 14 mm), LQFP128 (14 x 14 mm) and UFBGA121 (6 x 6 mm, 0.5 mm ball pitch). All are ECOPACK packages.

The top side carries the product identification on two lines, a date code (year and week), a revision code and a pin 1 or ball A1 mark; markings vary with the supply chain, and other optional marks are not shown. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, are not qualified for production use.

Each temperature suffix guarantees an ambient temperature at full dissipation and a maximum junction temperature (6: 85 °C ambient, 105 °C junction; 3: 125 °C ambient, 130 °C junction). Since an application rarely runs at full dissipation, work out the real dissipation and junction temperature and choose the suffix from those.

At TAmax 82 °C, IDDmax 50 mA at VDD 3.5 V, 20 outputs low at 8 mA with VOL 0.4 V and 8 outputs low at 20 mA with VOL 1.3 V: PINTmax = 175 mW, PI/Omax = 272 mW, PDmax = 447 mW. With 42 °C/W for LQFP100, TJmax = 82 + 18.774 = 100.774 °C, inside suffix 6 (junction up to 105 °C). At this dissipation the highest ambient is 86.226 °C for suffix 6 and 111.226 °C for suffix 3.

A part can run in a hot ambient if its dissipation is low enough to keep TJ in range. At TAmax 100 °C, IDDmax 20 mA at VDD 3.5 V and 20 outputs low at 8 mA with VOL 0.4 V: PINTmax = 70 mW, PI/Omax = 64 mW, PDmax = 134 mW. With 42 °C/W for LQFP100, TJmax = 100 + 5.628 = 105.628 °C, above suffix 6, so suffix 3 is needed unless the dissipation is cut to fit suffix 6.
